title: Why Do Some People Have Poor Judgment
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece deconstructs the vague label of 'poor judgment' into two distinct, learnable skills: accurately predicting how events will unfold, and accurately distinguishing high from low quality in people, products, and ideas. The author argues that both skills are grounded primarily in accumulated experience rather than raw intelligence, which is why judgment is notoriously hard to coach and takes years to develop, especially in an unfamiliar domain. The piece closes on the practical stakes: a reputation for poor judgment quietly stalls careers because others stop trusting the person with consequential decisions.
points: Judgment decomposes into two testable skills — predicting outcomes and discriminating quality — rather than being one vague trait.
Because judgment is rooted in accumulated experience rather than innate ability, it resists coaching and can take years to build in a new domain.
A reputation for poor judgment has a compounding career cost: people are quietly passed over for the assignments that would let them build better judgment.
quotes: Judgment, which is a critical stepping stone for making quality decisions, is reflected by two distinct skills: the ability to predict actions or responses as they unfold, and the ability to distinguish between high and low quality in assessing events, products, and ideas.
The more accurate a team member is in predicting what will happen next in any unfolding situation, the higher the quality of their judgment-making.
Developing these two skills of judgment is a long-term process and is often thought not to be very coachable.
However, experience is usually the missing link to advancing judgment skill. And that can’t easily be attained in short order.
Because judgment reflects our experience and knowledge, it quickly reveals what we don’t know.
